analysis.one_liner: Shields pre-K-12 teachers and administrators from most lawsuits in federal court.
analysis.headline: A single-sponsor bill with no cosponsors died in the House Judiciary Committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made school teachers, aides, librarians, principals, and superintendents immune from being sued for damages in federal court for anything they did on the job, whether in public or private schools. The only exceptions would be breaking a contract or committing a crime. It also would have required that a school employee who wins such a case be repaid for attorney fees, court costs, and out-of-pocket losses.
analysis.who_benefits: School personnel — teachers, aides, librarians, principals, and superintendents — and the public and private schools they work for. They would be protected from federal lawsuits over on-the-job acts, and could recover their legal costs when a case against them fails.
analysis.who_benefits_short: School staff and the schools they serve

how_it_helps.text: An educator or school administrator in any pre-K-12 school, public or private, would not be liable in federal court for damages or any other legal remedy for any act or omission in the course and scope of employment [S3].
The immunity would not cover liability under a contract or conduct punishable as a crime, so those claims could still be brought [S3].
A teacher or administrator who is sued and found not liable, or whose case is dismissed, would be reimbursed for attorneys fees, court costs, and out-of-pocket money lost from the litigation [S3].
The protection would extend to unpaid workers as well, since 'employed' is defined to include work on an unpaid basis [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Students and their families. If a teacher or administrator negligently injures a child or violates a child's rights at school, the family would be shut out of federal court, with recourse only in state court or in the narrow criminal and contract exceptions. Fee reimbursement could also add costs to families who sue and lose.
analysis.who_pays_short: Students and families seeking to sue schools

drawbacks.text: Families of children harmed by negligent educators would lose access to federal court remedies, keeping only state-court routes and the narrow exceptions for crimes and contract breaches [S3].

The fee-shifting provision would require reimbursement of legal costs whenever a school employee prevails, which could deter families from filing even strong claims because of the financial risk of losing [S3].
Because immunity would apply to public and private schools alike, including unpaid staff, the shield would be broad and hard to police beyond the crime and contract carve-outs [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Protecting school employees from litigation anxiety has some appeal, but this bill was a very blunt instrument: it granted near-total federal immunity to everyone from a guest lecturer to a superintendent, and its cost would fall on children and families who suffered real harm. Weighing broad loss of legal accountability for school misconduct against a diffuse benefit to staff, the costs clearly outweighed the benefits.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Louie Gohmert introduced the bill on December 19, 2007, near the end of the first session of the 110th Congress [S1][S5].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day, and no further action was ever recorded on it [S5].
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The bill's short title, 'Educational Immunity Act of 2005,' appears to carry over from an earlier Congress even though it was introduced in 2007 [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, students and families kept their ability to sue educators and school administrators in federal court, and no school employee or school gained the immunity it would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Students and families kept their day in court

for.name: Rep. Louie Gohmert
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Judiciary Committee; it had no other backers.

against.name: House Committee on the Judiciary
against.what_they_did: Took no action after receiving the referral — no hearing, no markup, and no vote was ever recorded on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Only one Republican member ever supported the bill and no one acted against it on the record, so no partisan lineup ever formed; it simply attracted no support.

industries.note: The bill would give them near-total immunity from federal lawsuits over their work, including unpaid staff. Their gain comes directly at the expense of families seeking remedies for harm done to children at school.
Schools and districts would face fewer lawsuits and lower litigation costs from employees' on-the-job conduct. The savings would come out of compensation for injured or wronged students.
Less exposure to federal-court claims would reduce payouts and premiums for insurers covering schools and staff. The protection would come from families losing access to that court system.
